replies.author: @SteifWood
replies.text:
@knuterikfønstelien ... well, it's pertinent to add some historical facts and political decisions to that: 

1) Panikkloven (Panic Act) in 1906 halted the acquisition of waterfalls and natural resources by foreign companies, 
2) Konsesjonsloven (Concession Act) in 1909 stipulated that private entities wishing to develop hydroelectric power had to apply for permits from the state,
3) Hjemfallsretten (Reversion Right/Industrial Concession Act) 1909-17 established that private ownership of hydroelectric power plants must be reverted to the public sector (state or municipalities) without compensation after a certain period (originally 60–80 years).
4) EFTA-domstolen (EEA/EFTA Court) ruled in 2007 that the current system was discriminatory because it applied only to private entities and not to public owners; hence, there was a
5) Lovendring (Legislative amendment) in 2008 where Stortinget (Norwegian Parliament) adopted adjustments to the Hjemfallsretten to align the rules with the EEA Agreement. New concessions for large waterfalls are now, as a general rule, granted only to the state, counties, or municipalities.

All in all, through these policy measures, the state and the people have become the owners of all profits from hydropower. This approach to public ownership was subsequently carried forward by politicians when oil was discovered; it was decided that all extraction would be based on licenses under which oil companies could not own the oil itself but instead had to pay a substantial tax on their profits — a tax that formed the foundation of Oljefondet (Government Pension Fund Global, i.e., the Oil Fund).


Adding to that, in 2001 Stortinget introduced Handlingsreglen (The Fiscal Rule), which is a guideline for government spending that governs the use of funds from Oljefondet. The main principle is that, over time, withdrawals should align with the fund's expected real return. The purpose is: 
a) long-term saving of the fund's real value so that future generations can also benefit from the money,
b) stabilizing the economy by phasing in oil revenues gradually and adjusting spending according to the economic climate (business cycles) of the given year. 
The rule was originally set at 4 percent, reduced to 3 percent in 2017 as it was too big for a healthy economy, and may be reduced to 2 - 2.5% in the coming years.

replies.author: @tessjuel
replies.text:
@GeomapUnveiled25 Thank you. Joke aside, I actually used to spend a lot of time on in the mountains, mostly on daytrips but nowadays I live in one of the relatively flat parts of Norway so although I still go on hikes almost every day, there are no mountains involved anymore.
A good video btw but a few corrections:
+ There are no polar bears in mainland Norway, only on Svalbard and Jan Mayen.
+ As much as I hate to admit it, even the highest peaks in Norway are dwarfed by the big mountains in the Alps. We're not even close.
+ The name Jotunheimen is actually quite recent, dating back only to 1820. Before that the area didn't have any particular name as was largely ignored.
+ We don't produce almost 100% of our electricity with water power anymore. We get quite a lot of solar and wind power too now. It's still almost exclusively renewable energy though.
+ Arguably neither Nordkapp nor Knivskjellodded are the northernmost point on contiental Europe since they both are on an island. The northernmost point of mainland Europe is Kinnarodden, about 120 km east of Nordkapp.
+ It's actually not only the North Atlantic current that keeps the Norwegian shores ice free. The Norwegaian Sea is very deep, between 1600 and 1800 m on average and 3950 m at its deepest. All that water works as a gigantic thermal battery absorbing heat in the summer and releasing it during the winter.
+ You show the Arctic Circle just south of Tromsø at 11:00. at 12:54 you show it much further south (yes, the Arctic Circle is the limit how far south we have the midnight sun at sea level; that's the definition of the Arctic Circle.) It's actually somewhere in between - a little bit south of Lofoten.
+ Norwegian overseas territories are even bigger than you think. It also includes Peter I's Island and Queen Maud Land. Peter I's Island is just 285 km2 but Queen Maud Land is 2 700 000 km2, almost as big as Argentina.
+ E6 is even longer than you think, It turns eastwards up north and goes all the way to Kirkenes, close to the Russian border.
